'''Victor John Emery''' (16 May 1934 – 17 July 2002)<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Tranquada |first=John |last2=Strongin |first2=Myron |last3=Johnson |first3=Peter |last4=Kivelson |first4=Steven |date=2004-10-01 |title=Victor John Emery |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/57/10/92/412389/Victor-John-Emery |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=57 |issue=10 |pages=92–93 |doi=10.1063/1.1825280 |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref> was a British specialist on [[superconductor]]s and [[superfluidity]]. His model for the electronic structure of the copper-oxide planes is the starting point for many analyses of high-temperature superconductors and is commonly known as the [[Emery model]].

==Early life==
Emery was born in [[Boston, Lincolnshire]], England.<ref name=":0" /> He went to study [[physics]] at the [[University of London]] (bachelor's degree in science in 1954) and the [[University of Manchester]], where he gained a PhD in [[theoretical physics]] under the supervision of [[Richard J. Eden]].<ref name=":0" />

==Career==
After completing his studies at Manchester he spent two years as a research associate at [[Cavendish Laboratory]] in [[Cambridge]].<ref name=":0" /> He was a Fellow at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] from 1959 to 1960.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Emery, V. J. (Victor J.) |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11508006.html |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref> While at Berkeley in 1960, together with [[Andrew Sessler]], he made the prediction that liquid [[helium-3]] would experience superfluidity by mechanism similar to the one of [[BCS theory]].<ref name=":0" /> The theory was later confirmed experimentally in 1972 by [[David Lee (physicist)|David Lee]], [[Douglas Osheroff]], and [[Robert Coleman Richardson]], who shared the 1996 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1960, Emery returned to the United Kingdom where he spent three years as a lecturer at the [[University of Birmingham]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Afterwards, Emery joined the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]'s Physics Department in 1964.<ref name=":0" /> After joining BNL, he worked on fundamental theories for the behaviour of helium-3/[[helium-4]] mixtures.<ref name=":0" />

Emery's work with low-temperature superconductivity laid the foundation for his concentration over the next nine years on the theory of [[high-temperature superconductivity]]. Discovered in 1986, high-temperature superconductors have the potential to bring superconducting technology into everyday use.

Emery presented one of the first theories, identifying the nature of the superconducting material's 'holes', which are the carriers of the supercurrent. He correctly stated that the holes tend to sit mainly on [[oxygen]], rather than on copper, contrary to initial popular belief.<ref name=":0" /> His model for the electronic structure of the copper-oxide planes is the starting point for many analyses of high-temperature superconductors and is commonly known as the [[Emery model]].

Emery received tenure at Brookhaven National Laboratory in 1967 and was named Senior Physicist in 1972.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> In the Physics Department he led the [[Cryogenics]] Group from 1973 to 1977 and the Solid State Theory Group from 1975 to 1984 and again from 1994.<ref name=":0" />

==Death==
By 2002, he had been suffering from [[amyotrophic lateral sclerosis]] (ALS) for two years. The progressive debility interfered with his work until finally he could no longer go to his office. He died on 17 July of that year.<ref name=":0" />

== Honors and awards ==
In 2001, Emery (with [[Alan Harold Luther|Alan H. Luther]]) won the [[Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]] for his "fundamental contribution to the theory of interacting electrons in a one-dimension". The theory is believed to be of crucial importance for understanding high temperature superconductors.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Greenberg |first=Diane |date=2001 |title=Victor Emery to Receive Buckley Prize in Condensed Matter |url=https://www.bnl.gov/bnlweb/pubaf/bulletin/files/2001/20010126.pdf |journal=The Bulletin |volume=55 |issue=2}}</ref>

On 13 October 2001, Emery became a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-10 |title=Victor J. Emery {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/victor-j-emery |access-date=2025-05-29 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref>
